newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Sweden accused of treating asylum seekers unfairly.
newsitem.headline: Sweden accused of treating asylum seekers unfairly.

text.p: A leading human rights group on Wednesday accused Sweden, long known for its open door immigration policy, of treating asylum seekers unfairly in recent years.
Human Rights Watch alleged that under its tough, new approach on immigration Sweden has rejected asylum seekers without giving their cases a fair hearing.

"In recent years Sweden has sent asylum seekers back to some of the world's worst trouble spots after concluding that their asylum claims were "manifestly unfounded'," a report by the U.S.-based group said.
It added that Sweden had set up a number of increasingly restrictive policies in reponse to a sharp rise in the number of asylum seekers in the 1990s.

Sweden had no limits to how long a person could be held in custody while decisions were made about their application, and, although not detained in bad conditions, they were treated like criminals, it said.
Some were held for more than a year," it added.
"Sweden detains some asylum seekers in remand prisons where they are fully integrated with common criminals and subject to a criminal detention regime," the report said.

Sweden's open-door immigration policy made it a haven for immigrants from the 1960s onwards and now nearly one in eight of the 8.8 million people living in Sweden are immigrants or have at least one immigrant parent.
But, with the break-up of the former Soviet Union and the conflict in the former Yugoslavia, the number of asylum seekers rose dramatically. Immigration peaked at 78,987 cases in 1994.
Sweden began toughening up its rules, limiting the number of immigrants, and the number fell to 32,486 in 1995.

"To escape poverty in hope of a better life is only human, but we cannot remove the injustices in the world by giving asylum to everyone who leaves their country to seek a better future," Immigration Minister Pierre Schori said recently.
New legislation put before parliament this month aims to clarify who will be accepted into Sweden and streamline the application process.
"A major reform of this policy is planned for this fall, with the government promising to pursue an even stricter asylum regime," the report said.
Rising unemployment, the recession and a growing resentment towards immigrants coincided with an influx of applicants and allowed restrictive policies to evolve, the report said.
Despite this many Swedes remain opposed to the changes.
